cover.title: 50 Most Asked API Interview Questions
cover.subtitle: 10 themed pages of 5, fundamentals to design scenarios
cover.tagline: For backend and SDE candidates: one-line answer, key points and a diagram, table or snippet each

blocks.q: Q1. What is a REST API and what are its constraints?
a_bullets: A ==REST== API exposes resources as URLs and acts on them with standard HTTP methods.
**Client-server**: UI and data storage evolve apart
**Stateless**: each request carries all it needs
**Cacheable**, **uniform interface**, **layered system**
Optional: code on demand (server sends scripts)

blocks.q: Q2. What is the difference between REST, GraphQL and gRPC?
a_bullets: REST uses many resource URLs, GraphQL one endpoint with client-shaped queries, gRPC typed ==Protobuf== calls.
REST: simple, cacheable, may over-fetch
GraphQL: client picks fields, avoids over-fetching
gRPC: binary and fast, suits internal services

blocks.q: Q3. What is the difference between HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3?
a_bullets: Each version moves the same HTTP semantics over a faster transport.
HTTP/1.1: text, one request at a time per connection
HTTP/2: binary, ==multiplexing==, header compression
HTTP/3: runs on QUIC over UDP, no TCP head-of-line blocking

blocks.q: Q4. What are the main parts of an HTTP request and response?
a_bullets: Both are a start line, headers and an optional body.
Request start line: **method**, path, version
Response start line: version, ==status code==, reason
Headers carry metadata like `Content-Type` and `Authorization`

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Stateless does not mean no database: state lives in the client token or shared storage, not in server memory.

blocks.q: Q5. What does it mean for an API to be stateless, and why does it matter?
a_bullets: The server keeps no client session between requests; each request holds everything needed, like a token.
Any server can answer any request, so scaling out is easy
Failures and restarts lose no session data
Cost: the client resends credentials each time

blocks.q: Q6. What is the difference between GET and POST?
a_bullets: ==GET== reads a resource; ==POST== sends data to create or trigger something.
GET is safe and cacheable; POST changes server state.
GET carries params in the URL, POST in the body.
Never put passwords in a GET URL: logs keep it.

blocks.q: Q7. What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
a_bullets: ==PUT== replaces the whole resource; ==PATCH== changes only some fields.
PUT is idempotent: same body, same final state.
A PUT that omits a field can erase it.
PATCH idempotency depends on how the patch is written.

blocks.q: Q8. Which HTTP methods are safe and which are idempotent?
a_bullets: __Safe__ means no state change; __idempotent__ means repeating gives the same end state.
Every safe method is also idempotent.
DELETE is idempotent but not safe.
POST is neither, so retries can duplicate.

blocks.q: Q9. What is the difference between 401 and 403?
a_bullets: **401** means unauthenticated: identity missing or invalid.
**403** means authenticated but not allowed.
401 should carry a `WWW-Authenticate` header.
Return 404 instead of 403 to hide a resource's existence.
Match the code to the outcome: success, client fault or server fault.
Use 2xx when the request worked, 4xx when the caller must fix it.
Use 5xx only for server bugs or outages, never for bad input.
Keep codes consistent across every endpoint.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Safe means read-only. Idempotent means retry-safe. 401 is who, 403 is what.

blocks.q: Q11. How does a JWT work and what are its three parts?
a_bullets: A JWT is a signed, self-contained token: the server verifies the signature and trusts the claims, with no lookup.
{blue:Header}: algorithm and type, e.g. `HS256`.
{green:Payload}: claims like `sub`, `exp`, `role`.
{red:Signature}: sign(header.payload, secret) detects tampering.
Payload is only base64url-encoded, **not encrypted**.

blocks.q: Q12. What is the difference between session-based and token-based authentication?
a_bullets: A session keeps state on the server and gives the client an opaque ID. A token carries the state itself, signed.
Sessions: easy to revoke, but need a shared store like Redis.
Tokens: stateless, scale across services, but hard to revoke.
Sessions suit server-rendered apps; tokens suit APIs and mobile.

blocks.q: Q13. Where should you store a JWT on the client: localStorage or a cookie?
a_bullets: Prefer an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite` cookie: JavaScript cannot read it, so an XSS bug cannot steal it.
localStorage is readable by any script on the page, so one XSS leaks the token.
Cookies are sent automatically, so add CSRF defence: `SameSite` or a CSRF token.

blocks.q: Q14. What is the difference between access tokens and refresh tokens?
a_bullets: An access token calls the API and is short-lived. A refresh token only gets new access tokens and lives longer.
Access: 5-15 min, sent on every request.
Refresh: days or weeks, sent only to the token endpoint.
Rotate refresh tokens and detect reuse to catch theft.

blocks.q: Q15. How do you revoke or invalidate a JWT before it expires?
a_bullets: A stateless JWT cannot be recalled, so you add a small piece of server state or keep the lifetime short.
Keep access tokens short and revoke the refresh token.
Denylist the token's `jti` until its `exp` passes.
Store a per-user token version and reject older ones.
Rotate the signing key to kill every token at once.

blocks.title: Interview takeaway
blocks.text: JWTs trade easy revocation for stateless scale. Fix that with short access tokens plus revocable refresh tokens.

blocks.q: Q16. What is OAuth 2.0 and what problem does it solve?
a_bullets: OAuth 2.0 is a ==delegation== framework: an app gets limited access to a user's data without ever seeing their password.
Solves the "give me your Gmail password" anti-pattern.
Roles: resource owner, client, authorization server, resource server
Access is scoped (`read:contacts`) and revocable
The password stays with the authorization server

blocks.q: Q17. What is the difference between authentication and authorization, and between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect?
a_bullets: __Authentication__ proves who you are; __authorization__ decides what you may do. OAuth 2.0 only does the second; ==OIDC== adds identity on top.
OIDC adds an `id_token` (a JWT about the user)
Request the `openid` scope to switch OIDC on
OAuth access token = a key card, not an ID badge
"Login with Google" is OIDC, not plain OAuth

blocks.q: Q18. Which OAuth 2.0 grant types exist and when do you use each?
a_bullets: A grant is how a client obtains a token; pick it by who the client is and whether a user is present.
==Authorization Code== (+PKCE): web, mobile and SPA apps with a user
==Client Credentials==: machine-to-machine, no user
Device Code: TVs and CLIs with no browser
Implicit and Password grants are **deprecated**

blocks.q: Q19. How does the Authorization Code flow with PKCE work?
a_bullets: The client sends the user to log in, gets a one-time ==code== back, then swaps it for tokens using a secret it generated itself.
PKCE stops a stolen code from being redeemed by an attacker
Client makes a random `code_verifier`
Sends its hash as `code_challenge` up front
Token call must present the original verifier

blocks.q: Q20. What is the difference between API keys, Basic auth and Bearer tokens?
a_bullets: All three put a credential in the request; they differ in what it identifies and how long it lives.
**API key**: identifies the app, long-lived, no user
**Basic**: base64 of `user:pass`, sent on every call
**Bearer**: any token in the header; anyone holding it gets in
Always use HTTPS: base64 is encoding, not encryption

blocks.title: Interview line
blocks.text: OAuth gives access, OIDC proves identity, PKCE protects the code.

items: Public clients (SPA, mobile) cannot keep a secret
Intercepted code is useless without the verifier
Skipping PKCE on a public client
Sending tokens in the redirect URL

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Say PKCE is now recommended for every client, even confidential ones.

blocks.q: Q21. What is CORS and why does the browser enforce it?
a_bullets: CORS lets a server say which ==origins== may read its responses; the browser enforces it to protect same-origin policy.
Origin = scheme + host + port (`app.io` ≠ `api.io`)
Server opts in via `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`
**Browser-only**: curl and servers ignore it
With cookies, never `*`; echo one exact origin

blocks.q: Q22. What is a preflight request and when is it sent?
a_bullets: A preflight is an automatic ==OPTIONS== request asking permission first; sent for non-simple requests.
Triggers: PUT, PATCH, DELETE, custom headers
Also `Content-Type: application/json`, `Authorization`
Cache with `Access-Control-Max-Age`
Simple GET/POST with form types skip it

blocks.q: Q23. What is the difference between CSRF and XSS, and how do you prevent each?
a_bullets: ==CSRF== tricks a logged-in browser into a forged request; ==XSS== injects script into your page.
CSRF fix: `SameSite` cookies + anti-CSRF tokens
XSS fix: output encoding + strict **CSP**
Bearer header tokens aren't auto-sent: CSRF-immune
XSS can steal tokens, bypass CSRF defences

blocks.q: Q24. How do you protect an API against OWASP API Top 10 risks like BOLA and injection?
a_bullets: Check ownership on **every** object access; never trust client input. ==BOLA== = changing an ID to read another user's object.
BOLA: verify object belongs to caller
Injection: parameterized queries + schema validation
Rate limits, least-privilege scopes, no mass assignment
Return 404, not 403, to hide IDs

blocks.title: Interview takeaway
blocks.text: CORS is a browser rule, not authentication: enforce BOLA checks and TLS on the server.

slides.page_title: Securing Data in Transit and at Rest

blocks.q: Q25. How do you secure an API in transit and at rest?
a_bullets: Encrypt the wire with ==TLS==, stored data with managed keys; hash passwords, don't encrypt.
Transit: HTTPS only, TLS 1.2+, HSTS, service mTLS
Rest: AES-256 disk/DB, keys in a KMS
Secrets in a vault, never code or logs
Passwords: bcrypt or argon2 + salt

slides.subtitle: Q21 to Q25

blocks.q: Q26. Offset vs cursor pagination?
a_bullets: ==Offset== skips N rows; ==cursor== resumes after the last item seen.
Offset can jump to page 5 but is slow on deep pages.
Offset drifts: inserts or deletes cause dupes or gaps.
Cursor is stable and fast via an indexed key; no random jumps.

blocks.q: Q27. Filtering, sorting and field selection in REST?
a_bullets: Use ==query parameters== on the collection URL.
Whitelist filter/sort fields; reject unknown ones with 400.
Prefix `-` for descending; comma lists for multiple keys.
`fields=` trims payloads; back sorts with an index.

blocks.q: Q28. What is rate limiting and why?
a_bullets: Caps requests per client per time window.
Stops abuse, brute force and ==noisy neighbours==.
Keeps cost and latency predictable under load.
Key by API key, user or IP; tier per plan.

blocks.q: Q29. Token bucket vs leaky bucket vs sliding window?
a_bullets: Each trades burst tolerance against smoothness and memory.
**Token bucket**: tokens refill steadily; a request spends one, so bursts pass.
**Leaky bucket**: requests queue, drain at a fixed rate.
**Sliding window**: counts last N seconds, avoiding boundary spikes.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Cursor for feeds, offset for small admin lists; name your limiter's key.

blocks.q: Q30. What should a 429 contain; how do clients react?
a_bullets: Return ==429 Too Many Requests==, `Retry-After` and a clear error body.
Send `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `-Remaining`, `-Reset` on every response.
Clients stop, wait `Retry-After`, then retry.
Use exponential backoff with ==jitter==; never loop tightly.

blocks.q: Q31. How does HTTP caching work with Cache-Control, ETag and Last-Modified?
a_bullets: The server tells clients how long a response is ==fresh==; after that they revalidate instead of refetching.
`Cache-Control: max-age=60` means reuse it for 60s, no request sent
`ETag` is a version fingerprint; client replays it in `If-None-Match`
`Last-Modified` is the date-based twin, sent back as `If-Modified-Since`
Unchanged data gives a **304** with no body, which saves bandwidth

blocks.q: Q32. What is the difference between client-side, CDN and server-side caching?
a_bullets: They cache at different distances from the user: ==browser==, ==edge== or ==your own backend==.
Client cache is private to one user and costs zero network
CDN caches public responses at edge nodes near users
Server cache (Redis) saves database work for every caller
Use `private` for user data and `public` for shared data

blocks.q: Q34. What is an API gateway and what does it do?
a_bullets: An API gateway is the ==single entry point== in front of your services; it routes and enforces policy.
Authenticates callers (JWT, API keys) before traffic reaches services
Applies rate limiting, TLS termination and request logging
Routes `/orders` and `/users` to separate backends
Can transform, aggregate and cache responses

blocks.q: Q35. What is the difference between an API gateway, a load balancer and a reverse proxy?
a_bullets: A ==reverse proxy== fronts servers; a ==load balancer== is one that spreads traffic; a gateway adds API logic.
Reverse proxy: hides backends, terminates TLS, caches (nginx)
Load balancer: spreads requests across identical instances for scale
Gateway: auth, quotas, routing by path, versioning per API
They often stack: gateway sits in front of balancers

blocks.title: Say this in the interview
blocks.text: Cache close to the user, invalidate with a TTL plus explicit deletes, and put policy in the gateway.

blocks.q: Q33. What is cache invalidation and which strategies exist: cache-aside, write-through, write-back?
a_bullets: Invalidation means removing or updating cached data once the source changes, so reads are not stale.
**Cache-aside**: app reads cache, on a miss loads the DB and fills it
**Write-through**: every write goes to cache and DB together
**Write-back**: write cache first, flush to DB later; risks data loss
TTLs are the safety net when explicit invalidation is missed

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Delete the key on write instead of updating it: it avoids racing writers caching stale data.

blocks.q: Q36. What is a webhook and how does it differ from polling?
a_bullets: A ==webhook== is an HTTP callback: the provider POSTs to your URL the moment an event happens. Polling makes the client ask repeatedly.
**Push** means near-real-time and no wasted calls.
Polling is simpler and works behind firewalls.
Webhook receivers need a public HTTPS endpoint.

blocks.q: Q37. How do you make webhook delivery reliable and secure?
a_bullets: Sign every payload, retry failures with backoff, and have receivers dedupe by event ID.
**Sign** with HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body plus a timestamp.
Receiver returns 2xx fast, then processes async.
Retry with exponential backoff, then dead-letter queue.
Use HTTPS only and reject stale timestamps.

blocks.q: Q38. How do you make a POST request idempotent?
a_bullets: POST is not idempotent by default. Let the client send an ==Idempotency-Key== header and have the server store the first result.
Replays with the same key return the **saved** response.
Store key, request hash and response with a TTL.
Same key with a different body returns 422 or 409.
Enforce with a unique DB constraint.

blocks.q: Q39. What are the API versioning strategies and their trade-offs?
a_bullets: Pick one place to carry the version: the URL, a header, or the media type. Evolve additively inside a version.
**URL path** is the most visible and cache-friendly.
Header or media type keeps URLs clean but is hidden.
Query param is easy but easy to forget.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Retries are only safe when receivers are idempotent. Pair Q37 with Q38.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Only bump the version for breaking changes: adding a field is not one, removing or renaming one is.

blocks.q: Q40. How do you deprecate an API version without breaking clients?
a_bullets: Announce early, signal in responses, give a long overlap window, then sunset with a clear error.
Send `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers on every response.
Track per-client usage and contact heavy users.
After sunset return **410 Gone** with a migration link.

slides.page_title: File Uploads and the Test Pyramid

blocks.text: ★ 1. Large file uploads

blocks.q: Q41. How do you handle large file uploads in an API?
a_bullets: Never buffer the whole file in memory: ==stream== it in chunks, or let the client upload straight to storage.
Use **resumable** chunked uploads so a dropped connection restarts at the last chunk.
Cap size and check type server-side; never trust the filename.
Scan for malware, then process async and return 202.

blocks.text: ★ 2. multipart vs presigned

blocks.q: Q42. What is the difference between multipart/form-data uploads and direct-to-storage presigned URL uploads?
a_bullets: ==multipart/form-data== sends the file through your API server; a ==presigned URL== lets the client PUT it straight to S3.
Presigned keeps big bytes off your servers, so it scales and costs less.
The URL is short-lived and scoped to one key, method and size.
Multipart is simpler for small files, but ties up workers.

blocks.text: ★ 3. Test pyramid for APIs

blocks.q: Q43. What is the difference between unit, integration and contract tests for APIs?
a_bullets: ==Unit== tests one function with mocks; ==integration== tests the API with a real DB; ==contract== tests the agreed request and response shape.
Unit tests are fast and many; integration are fewer and slower.
Contract tests (Pact) catch breaking changes between consumer and provider.
Run contract tests in CI before every deploy.

blocks.text: ★ 4. What to monitor

blocks.q: Q44. What are the key metrics to monitor for an API: RED and the four golden signals?
a_bullets: ==RED== is Rate, Errors, Duration per service; the ==four golden signals== add Saturation to latency, traffic and errors.
Alert on p95 or p99 latency, never the average.
Split errors into 4xx (client) and 5xx (yours).
Saturation means CPU, memory, connection pool or queue depth.

items: Set an SLO, alert on error-budget burn
Put RED graphs at the top of dashboards

slides.subtitle: Q41 to Q45

blocks.text: ★ 5. Three pillars

blocks.q: Q45. What is the difference between logging, metrics and distributed tracing?
a_bullets: ==Logs== record single events, ==metrics== are numeric aggregates over time, ==traces== follow one request across services.
Metrics say something is wrong; traces show where; logs show why.
Share a trace ID in every log line to link all three.
Log structured JSON, never secrets or tokens.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Answer with a flow: alert on metrics, find the slow span in a trace, read the logs.

blocks.q: Q46. How do you scale an API horizontally to handle 10x traffic?
a_bullets: Run many identical ==stateless== instances behind a load balancer, and add more as load grows.
Keep session state in Redis or a DB, never in instance memory
Autoscale on CPU or request rate, not a fixed count
Cache reads and scale the database separately: replicas, sharding

blocks.q: Q47. How do you handle a slow or failing downstream dependency with timeouts, retries and a circuit breaker?
a_bullets: Never wait forever: ==timeout== each call, retry only safe failures, and ==trip a breaker== when errors pile up.
Set a timeout below your own caller's deadline
Retry with exponential backoff plus jitter, max 3 tries
Retry only idempotent calls, or ones with an idempotency key
Open breaker: fail fast or serve a fallback

blocks.q: Q48. What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous APIs, and when do you return 202 Accepted?
a_bullets: A sync API ==answers with the result== on the same request; an async API accepts the work and finishes it later.
Return **202** when work outlasts a normal request, like video encoding or reports
Body carries a job id; ==Location== header points to a status URL
Client polls the status URL or receives a webhook on completion

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Name the failure mode first, then the fix: timeout, retry, breaker, idempotency key.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: For payments, say idempotency key plus unique constraint before anything else.

blocks.q: Q49. How would you design a URL shortener API?
a_bullets: Two endpoints: create a short code for a long URL, and redirect a code to its target.
Code: base62 of a unique counter ID, 7 chars gives about 3.5 trillion
Redirect with **301** if permanent, **302** if you track clicks
Read-heavy: cache hot codes in Redis, store code to URL in a key-value DB
Validate URLs and rate limit creation to block abuse

blocks.q: Q50. How would you design a payment API that must never double-charge?
a_bullets: Make every charge ==idempotent==: the same key always returns the same result, never a second charge.
Client sends an `Idempotency-Key`; server stores key plus response
Wrap charge and key insert in one DB transaction with a unique constraint
Confirm final state via the provider webhook, and reconcile nightly
Retry on timeout with the same key, never a new one

caption.text:
50 API questions they will ask you in your next backend interview. 🎯

If you're prepping for an SDE or backend role, APIs come up in almost every round. This handbook is a fundamentals-to-advanced bank of the 50 most asked questions, in handwritten notes you can revise fast.

What's inside:
📌 REST and HTTP fundamentals
📌 Methods and status codes
📌 JWT and session authentication
📌 OAuth 2.0 and authorization
📌 CORS and API security
📌 Pagination, filtering and rate limiting
📌 Caching and API gateways
📌 Webhooks, idempotency and versioning
📌 File uploads, testing and monitoring
📌 Scalability and real-world design scenarios
📌 A one-page API interview cheatsheet

Save this for your next prep session and send it to the friend who's interviewing this month.

Which API question do you find the hardest? Tell us in the comments 👇
